s: King Manasseh, in chains, confesses his many sins and begs God for mercy, trusting in his great compassion.
i: Manasseh was one of the worst kings of Judah: the Bible says he set up idols in the Temple and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood. 2 Chronicles 33 tells how he was taken in chains to Babylon, humbled himself before God, prayed, and was brought home again. The Chronicler mentions that his prayer was written down, but the Bible does not give its words.

This short psalm of repentance claims to be that prayer. It was probably written by a Jewish author in the last centuries before Christ. Greek Bibles kept it among their odes, and the Latin Vulgate printed it after the Bible, which is why the 1609 Douay kept it in its appendix. The Church has never received it as Scripture, though Christians have long prayed it.

What to expect: one chapter of fifteen verses. Manasseh praises God the Creator, confesses that his sins are more than the sand of the sea, and asks for mercy, trusting that God is “the God of those who repent”.
